claim: Voice-onset time (VOT) is defined as the interval between a stop consonant's release and the onset of vocal fold vibration.
source: For example, voice-onset time (VOT), defined as the interval between a stop consonant's release and the onset of vocal fold vibration (acoustically, the burst and the voicing), is a critical cue that listeners use to distinguish voiced (e.g., /b/, /d/, /g/) from voiceless (e.g., /p/, /t/, /k/) stop consonants in English (Liberman et al., 1958; Lisker and Abramson, 1964).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text with supporting citations to prior work.

claim: VOT is a critical cue that listeners use to distinguish voiced from voiceless stop consonants in English.
source: For example, voice-onset time (VOT), defined as the interval between a stop consonant's release and the onset of vocal fold vibration (acoustically, the burst and the voicing), is a critical cue that listeners use to distinguish voiced (e.g., /b/, /d/, /g/) from voiceless (e.g., /p/, /t/, /k/) stop consonants in English (Liberman et al., 1958; Lisker and Abramson, 1964).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to foundational work on VOT perception.

claim: When the burst and voicing are roughly coincident (short VOT; ~0 ms), listeners perceive a bilabial stop as a /b/.
source: When the burst and voicing are roughly coincident (short VOT; ~0 ms), listeners perceive a bilabial stop as a /b/, but when voicing follows the burst after a temporal gap (long VOT; ~50 ms), listeners hear a /p/.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and reflects established knowledge about VOT perception.

claim: When voicing follows the burst after a temporal gap (long VOT; ~50 ms), listeners hear a /p/.
source: When the burst and voicing are roughly coincident (short VOT; ~0 ms), listeners perceive a bilabial stop as a /b/, but when voicing follows the burst after a temporal gap (long VOT; ~50 ms), listeners hear a /p/.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and reflects established knowledge about VOT perception.

claim: Information about a speech sound's identity is encoded in the amplitude of neural activity at phonetically-tuned cortical sites in the superior temporal gyrus (STG).
source: Recent evidence from human electrocorticography (ECoG) has shown that information about a speech sound's identity is encoded in the amplitude of neural activity at phonetically-tuned cortical sites in the superior temporal gyrus (STG) (Mesgarani et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior ECoG work.

claim: Distinct neural populations in STG respond selectively to different classes of phonemes that share certain spectral cues.
source: Distinct neural populations in this region respond selectively to different classes of phonemes that share certain spectral cues, such as the burst associated with stop consonants or the characteristic formant structure of vowels produced with specific vocal tract configurations.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and reflects prior findings about phonetic selectivity in STG.

claim: The exact VOT of a given utterance of a /b/ or a /p/ will vary considerably depending on numerous factors such as speech rate, phonetic context, and speaker accent.
source: In addition to distinguishing phonetic categories, the exact VOT of a given utterance of a /b/ or a /p/ will vary considerably depending on numerous factors such as speech rate, phonetic context, and speaker accent (Miller et al., 1986; Kessinger and Blumstein, 1997; Klatt, 1975; Lisker and Abramson, 1967; Allen et al., 2003; Flege and Eefting, 1986; Fox et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting sources of VOT variability.

claim: Sensitivity to fine-grained sub-phonetic detail is crucial for robust speech perception, allowing listeners to flexibly adapt and to integrate multiple cues to phonetic identity online in noisy, unstable environments.
source: Although only categorical phonetic identity (e.g., whether a particular VOT is more consistent with a /b/ or a /p/) is strictly necessary for understanding meaning, sensitivity to fine-grained sub-phonetic detail (e.g., whether a particular /p/ was pronounced with a 40 ms vs. a 50 ms VOT) is also crucial for robust speech perception, allowing listeners to flexibly adapt and to integrate multiple cues to phonetic identity online in noisy, unstable environments (Miller and Volaitis, 1989; Clayards et al., 2008; Kleinschmidt and Jaeger, 2015; McMurray and Jongman, 2011; Toscano and McMurray, 2010; Fox and Blumstein, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to work on perceptual adaptation and cue integration.

claim: Listeners are sensitive to sub-phonetic detail in speech sounds.
source: However, the neurophysiological mechanisms that support listeners' sensitivity (Kuhl, 1991; Carney, 1977; Pisoni and Tash, 1974; Massaro and Cohen, 1983; Andruski et al., 1994; McMurray et al., 2002; Schouten et al., 2003) to such detailed speech representations are not known.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting behavioral sensitivity to sub-phonetic detail.

claim: Participants listened to and categorized speech sounds from a digitally synthesized continuum of consonant-vowel syllables that differed linearly only in their voice-onset time (VOT) from /ba/ (0 ms VOT) to /pa/ (50 ms VOT).
source: Participants listened to and categorized speech sounds from a digitally synthesized continuum of consonant-vowel syllables that differed linearly only in their voice-onset time (VOT) from /ba/ (0 ms VOT) to /pa/ (50 ms VOT).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental stimuli used in the study.

claim: The six-step VOT continuum was constructed by manipulating only the relative timing of the spectral burst and the onset of voicing while holding all other acoustic properties of the stimuli constant.
source: This six-step continuum was constructed by manipulating only the relative timing of the spectral burst and the onset of voicing while holding all other acoustic properties of the stimuli constant (Figure 1A/B; see Materials and methods) (Klatt, 1980).
evidence: The claim describes the stimulus construction method and references Figure 1A/B showing the stimuli.

claim: Stimuli with longer VOTs were more often labeled as /pa/.
source: Analysis of participants' identification behavior confirmed that stimuli with longer VOTs were more often labeled as /pa/ (mixed effects logistic regression: βVOT = 0.19, t = 17.78, p=5.6*10−63; data for example participant in Figure 1C; data for all participants in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and references to figures showing the results.

claim: Listeners' perception of the linear VOT continuum was sharply non-linear, a behavioral hallmark of categorical perception.
source: Moreover, and consistent with past work, listeners' perception of the linear VOT continuum was sharply non-linear, a behavioral hallmark of categorical perception (Liberman et al., 1957; Liberman et al., 1961; Kronrod et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data and citations to prior work on categorical perception.

claim: A psychophysical category boundary between 20 ms and 30 ms divided the continuum into stimuli most often perceived as voiced (/b/: 0 ms, 10 ms, 20 ms VOTs) or as voiceless (/p/: 30 ms, 40 ms, 50 ms VOTs).
source: A psychophysical category boundary between 20 ms and 30 ms divided the continuum into stimuli most often perceived as voiced (/b/: 0 ms, 10 ms, 20 ms VOTs) or as voiceless (/p/: 30 ms, 40 ms, 50 ms VOTs).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of behavioral identification data.

claim: 49 VOT-sensitive sites were found, primarily located over the lateral mid-to-posterior STG, bilaterally.
source: Across all participants, we found 49 VOT-sensitive sites, primarily located over the lateral mid-to-posterior STG, bilaterally.
evidence: The claim reports the number and location of VOT-sensitive electrodes identified in the study.

claim: Peak response amplitude at VOT-sensitive electrodes reliably discriminated between voicing categories, exhibiting stronger responses to either voiced (/b/; VOT = 0–20 ms; n = 33) or voiceless (/p/; VOT = 30–50 ms; n = 16) stimuli.
source: Peak response amplitude at these VOT-sensitive electrodes reliably discriminated between voicing categories, exhibiting stronger responses to either voiced (/b/; VOT = 0–20 ms; n = 33) or voiceless (/p/; VOT = 30–50 ms; n = 16) stimuli (Figure 1D; locations of all sites shown in Figures 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by neural data analysis and references to figures showing electrode locations and selectivity.

claim: Within individual participants, electrodes spaced only 4 mm apart showed strong preferences for different voicing categories.
source: We observed that, within individual participants, electrodes spaced only 4 mm apart showed strong preferences for different voicing categories, and we did not observe any clear overall regional or hemispheric patterns in the prevalence or selectivity patterns of VOT-sensitive electrodes (see Materials and methods for additional information).
evidence: The claim is based on spatial analysis of electrode selectivity patterns.

claim: Robust category selectivity in voiceless-selective (V-) and voiced-selective (V+) neural populations emerged as early as 50–150 ms post-stimulus onset and often lasted for several hundred milliseconds.
source: Robust category selectivity in voiceless-selective (V-) and voiced-selective (V+) neural populations emerged as early as 50–150 ms post-stimulus onset and often lasted for several hundred milliseconds (example electrodes in Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim describes the temporal dynamics of category selectivity and references Figure 1E showing example time courses.

claim: Voicing category selectivity was reliable whether a trial's voicing category was defined based on the psychophysically-determined category boundary or based on the actual behavioral response recorded for each trial.
source: Across all VOT-sensitive electrodes, voicing category selectivity was reliable whether a trial's voicing category was defined based on the psychophysically-determined category boundary (0–20 ms vs. 30–50 ms VOTs; V- electrodes: z = 3.52, p=4.4×10−4; V+ electrodes: z = −5.01, p=5.4×10−7; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests) or based on the actual behavioral response recorded for each trial (V- electrodes: p=4.9×10−4; V+ electrodes: p=6.1×10−5; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical tests on neural data using two different definitions of voicing category.

claim: Spatially distinct neural populations in auditory cortex are tuned to speech sound categories defined by a temporal cue.
source: These results show that spatially distinct neural populations in auditory cortex are tuned to speech sound categories defined by a temporal cue.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the neural data showing category-selective responses.

claim: If individual neural populations only responded to spectral features, we would not have observed overall amplitude differences in their responses to /b/ versus /p/ categories.
source: Critically, if individual neural populations only responded to spectral features (e.g., to the burst or to the onset of voicing), we would not have observed overall amplitude differences in their responses to /b/ versus /p/ categories.
evidence: The claim is a logical inference about what the results imply regarding temporal integration.

claim: Across participants, classification accuracy for voicing category was significantly better than chance.
source: We found that, across participants, classification accuracy was significantly better than chance (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.016; Figure 1F, leftmost box plot), demonstrating that spatially and temporally distributed population neural activity during the peak response contains information that allows for decoding of a temporally-cued phonetic distinction in speech.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of classifier performance and references Figure 1F showing the results.

claim: Spatially and temporally distributed population neural activity during the peak response contains information that allows for decoding of a temporally-cued phonetic distinction in speech.
source: We found that, across participants, classification accuracy was significantly better than chance (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.016; Figure 1F, leftmost box plot), demonstrating that spatially and temporally distributed population neural activity during the peak response contains information that allows for decoding of a temporally-cued phonetic distinction in speech.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the successful classification of voicing category from neural data.

claim: When the classifiers had access to amplitude information but not timing information during the peak response, performance was significantly better than chance.
source: Across participants, we found that, when the classifiers had access to amplitude information but not timing information (+Amplitude/-Timing) during the peak response, performance was significantly better than chance (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.016; Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of classifier performance with corrupted timing information.

claim: Classification accuracy with amplitude information alone was statistically comparable to the model that had access to both amplitude and timing information.
source: Furthermore, despite the profound corruption of temporal information in the neural responses, classification accuracy was statistically comparable to the model that had access to both amplitude and timing information (+Amplitude/+Timing; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.69; Figure 1F), suggesting that amplitude information alone is sufficient for classifying a trial's voicing category.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of classifier performance under different conditions.

claim: Amplitude information alone is sufficient for classifying a trial's voicing category.
source: Furthermore, despite the profound corruption of temporal information in the neural responses, classification accuracy was statistically comparable to the model that had access to both amplitude and timing information (+Amplitude/+Timing; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.69; Figure 1F), suggesting that amplitude information alone is sufficient for classifying a trial's voicing category.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the classifier performance results.

claim: When amplitude information was corrupted and only temporal patterns in the peak response window were reliable, classifier performance was not different from chance.
source: In contrast, when amplitude information was corrupted and only temporal patterns in the peak response window were reliable (-Amplitude/+Timing), classifier performance was not different from chance (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.69; Figure 1F) and was worse for every participant compared to the model with both types of information (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.016).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of classifier performance with corrupted amplitude information.

claim: Preserving timing information alone had no effect on classification performance compared to the most impoverished model where both amplitude and timing information were corrupted.
source: Finally, we compared the model with only timing information to a model where both amplitude and timing information during the peak window were corrupted (-Amplitude/-Timing). We found that preserving timing information alone had no effect on classification performance compared to the most impoverished model (-Amplitude/-Timing; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.58; Figure 1F), which also failed to perform better than chance (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.94; Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of classifier performance under different conditions.

claim: Localized peak high-gamma response amplitude spatially encodes voicing of single trials in STG, analogous to other spectrally-cued phonetic features.
source: Together, these results constitute evidence for a spatial/amplitude code for speech categories that differ in a temporal cue. Thus, localized peak high-gamma response amplitude spatially encodes voicing of single trials in STG, analogous to other spectrally-cued phonetic features (Mesgarani et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the classifier results and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Across all V- and V+ electrodes, peak high-gamma response amplitude encoded stimulus VOT within the preferred category but not the non-preferred category.
source: Across all V- and V+ electrodes, peak high-gamma response amplitude encoded stimulus VOT within the preferred category (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 6.02, p=1.7×10−9), but not the non-preferred category (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 1.31, p=0.19).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of within-category VOT encoding.

claim: V- electrodes encoded sub-phonetic VOT more robustly within the voiceless category than within the voiced category.
source: While V- electrodes encoded sub-phonetic VOT more robustly within the voiceless category than within the voiced category (Figure 2D, left; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 3.00, p=2.7×10−3), the opposite pattern emerged for V+ electrodes, which encoded sub-phonetic VOT more robustly within the voiced category than within the voiceless category (Figure 2D, right; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 3.78, p=1.6×10−4).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and references Figure 2D showing the encoding patterns.

claim: V+ electrodes encoded sub-phonetic VOT more robustly within the voiced category than within the voiceless category.
source: While V- electrodes encoded sub-phonetic VOT more robustly within the voiceless category than within the voiced category (Figure 2D, left; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 3.00, p=2.7×10−3), the opposite pattern emerged for V+ electrodes, which encoded sub-phonetic VOT more robustly within the voiced category than within the voiceless category (Figure 2D, right; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 3.78, p=1.6×10−4).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and references Figure 2D showing the encoding patterns.

claim: VOT encoding in human STG is not purely categorical.
source: Together, these analyses revealed two key results: (1) VOT encoding in human STG is not purely categorical, but also (2) the relationship between response amplitude and VOT is not linear across the entire continuum (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the within-category encoding analysis.

claim: The relationship between response amplitude and VOT is not linear across the entire continuum.
source: Together, these analyses revealed two key results: (1) VOT encoding in human STG is not purely categorical, but also (2) the relationship between response amplitude and VOT is not linear across the entire continuum (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the within-category encoding analysis and references Figure 2D.

claim: Individual neural populations in human auditory cortex encode information about both the category identity of a speech sound and its more fine-grained acoustic properties, or its category goodness.
source: These results suggest that, even at the level of STG, the brain maintains information about the specific, sub-phonetic details of individual speech sounds. The asymmetrical pattern of within-category encoding suggests that individual neural populations in human auditory cortex encode information about both the category identity of a speech sound and its more fine-grained acoustic properties, or its category goodness (Kuhl, 1991; Blumstein et al., 2005; Myers, 2007).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the asymmetric within-category encoding pattern and is supported by citations.

claim: A temporal cue that distinguishes speech sounds is represented by a spatial/amplitude code in human STG.
source: Thus far, we have demonstrated that a temporal cue that distinguishes speech sounds is represented by a spatial/amplitude code (Ferster and Spruston, 1995; Shadlen and Newsome, 1994) in human STG.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main finding and is supported by citations to prior work on spatial/amplitude coding.

claim: The entire neural network model is comprised of just five localist units: a burst detector, a voicing detector, a gap detector (Gap), a coincidence detector (Coinc), and an inhibitory unit.
source: The entire model is comprised of just five localist units: a burst detector, a voicing detector, a gap detector (Gap), a coincidence detector (Coinc), and an inhibitory unit.
evidence: The claim describes the architecture of the computational model.

claim: There are striking qualitative similarities between Gap simulated outputs and the real neural responses of V- electrodes.
source: The simulated responses of Gap and Coinc to VOTs of 0–50 ms are shown in Figure 2F/G. We observed striking qualitative similarities between Gap simulated outputs (Figure 2F) and the real neural responses of V- electrodes (Figure 2B), and between Coinc outputs (Figure 2G) and the V+ electrodes (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of model simulations to neural data shown in figures.

claim: There are striking qualitative similarities between Coinc outputs and the V+ electrodes.
source: The simulated responses of Gap and Coinc to VOTs of 0–50 ms are shown in Figure 2F/G. We observed striking qualitative similarities between Gap simulated outputs (Figure 2F) and the real neural responses of V- electrodes (Figure 2B), and between Coinc outputs (Figure 2G) and the V+ electrodes (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of model simulations to neural data shown in figures.

claim: Spatial encoding of temporal cues (gaps vs. coincidences) can arise naturally within a simple, biologically-inspired neural network.
source: By design, voicing category is clearly distinguished in both Gap and Coinc, with Gap responding more strongly to longer (voiceless) VOTs (30–50 ms), and Coinc responding more strongly to shorter (voiced) VOTs (0–20 ms). This demonstrates that spatial encoding of temporal cues (gaps vs. coincidences) can arise naturally within a simple, biologically-inspired neural network (Buonomano and Merzenich, 1995; Gao and Wehr, 2015; Eggermont, 2000; Carr, 1993; Konishi, 2003; Rauschecker, 2014; Rauschecker, 1998).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the model simulations and is supported by citations to prior work on temporal processing.

claim: Both Gap and Coinc detector units exhibit sensitivity to within-category VOT distinctions.
source: Perhaps more surprisingly, we also found that both Gap and Coinc detector units exhibit sensitivity to within-category VOT distinctions (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of model outputs shown in Figure 2H.

claim: V- electrodes and Gap units are only sensitive to differences among long (voiceless) VOTs.
source: These partially graded activations mirror the pattern observed in the neural data (Figure 2D), where V- electrodes and Gap units are only sensitive to differences among long (voiceless) VOTs, and V+ electrodes and Coinc units are only sensitive to differences among short (voiced) VOTs.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of model outputs to neural data patterns.

claim: V+ electrodes and Coinc units are only sensitive to differences among short (voiced) VOTs.
source: These partially graded activations mirror the pattern observed in the neural data (Figure 2D), where V- electrodes and Gap units are only sensitive to differences among long (voiceless) VOTs, and V+ electrodes and Coinc units are only sensitive to differences among short (voiced) VOTs.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of model outputs to neural data patterns.

claim: The timing of the evoked neural responses (relative to burst onset) appeared to depend on stimulus VOT in V+ electrodes and in the coincidence detector (Coinc) unit, but not in V- electrodes or in the gap detector (Gap) unit.
source: However, in comparing the real and simulated neural data (Figure 2), we also observed a qualitative resemblance with respect to the onset latencies of evoked responses. Specifically, the timing of the evoked neural responses (relative to burst onset) appeared to depend on stimulus VOT in V+ electrodes and in the coincidence detector (Coinc) unit (Figure 2C/G), but not in V- electrodes or in the gap detector (Gap) unit (Figure 2B/F).
evidence: The claim is based on visual comparison of neural data and model simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Response onset latency was strongly associated with VOT for V+, but not V-, electrodes.
source: We found that response onset latency was strongly associated with VOT for V+, but not V-, electrodes (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests: V+, p=1.6×10−6; V-, p=0.57), and this difference between the two electrode types was highly reliable (Mann-Whitney rank-sum test: p=1.7×10−5) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of onset latency data and references Figure 3B.

claim: The same well-established physiological mechanisms that give rise to peak amplitude encoding of temporally-cued voicing categories also predict the early temporal dynamics observed in real neural data.
source: Thus, the same well-established physiological mechanisms that give rise to peak amplitude encoding of temporally-cued voicing categories also predict the early temporal dynamics we observe in real neural data.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the model's ability to capture both amplitude and temporal dynamics.

claim: Both sub-phonetic and phonetic category-level information are carried by the onset latency of V+ electrodes.
source: Finally, Figure 3 shows that, unlike during the peak response window (150–250 ms after stimulus onset; Figure 1F), temporal information does encode VOT during an earlier window around the neural response onset in some neural populations. Indeed, both sub-phonetic and phonetic category-level information are carried by the onset latency of V+ electrodes, with evoked responses arising later at these sites for stimuli with progressively longer VOTs.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of onset latency data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Both the amplitude encoding patterns during the peak window and the temporal encoding patterns during the earlier onset window are captured by the same canonical neurophysiological mechanisms.
source: Critically, the modeling results indicate that both the amplitude encoding patterns during the peak window and the temporal encoding patterns during the earlier onset window are captured by the same canonical neurophysiological mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the model's ability to capture multiple aspects of the neural data.

claim: Discrete neural populations located primarily on the bilateral posterior and middle STG respond preferentially to either voiced sounds or voiceless sounds.
source: Using direct intracranial recordings, we found discrete neural populations located primarily on the bilateral posterior and middle STG that respond preferentially to either voiced sounds, where the onset of voicing is coincident with the burst or follows it after a short lag (20 ms or less), or voiceless sounds, where the onset of voicing follows the burst after a temporal gap of at least 30–50 ms.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding about neural population selectivity.

claim: The cortical representation of both spectral and temporal cues in speech follow a common spatial coding scheme.
source: The present results extend these earlier findings in a critical way, suggesting that the cortical representation of both spectral and temporal cues in speech follow a common spatial coding scheme.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the current results in the context of prior work.

claim: The digitally synthesized VOT stimuli were tightly controlled to vary only in the relative timing of two invariant spectral cues (burst and voicing).
source: This result is also consistent with prior reports that neural response amplitude depends on VOT (Mesgarani et al., 2014), but such results have often involved natural speech stimuli where voicing categories varied along many other spectral acoustic dimensions besides the temporal cue (Lisker, 1986; Soli, 1983; Stevens and Klatt, 1974; Summerfield and Haggard, 1977). Here, the digitally synthesized VOT stimuli were tightly controlled to vary only in the relative timing of two invariant spectral cues (burst and voicing), thereby demonstrating that this temporal speech cue is encoded in the peak high-gamma response amplitude of spatially distinct neural populations in human STG.
evidence: The claim describes the stimulus control used in the study and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: This temporal speech cue is encoded in the peak high-gamma response amplitude of spatially distinct neural populations in human STG.
source: Here, the digitally synthesized VOT stimuli were tightly controlled to vary only in the relative timing of two invariant spectral cues (burst and voicing), thereby demonstrating that this temporal speech cue is encoded in the peak high-gamma response amplitude of spatially distinct neural populations in human STG.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the neural data with controlled stimuli.

claim: Temporal and amplitude codes for VOT are not mutually exclusive.
source: Our examination of the timing and amplitude of three peaks in the auditory evoked local field potentials of VOT-sensitive electrodes confirmed that such patterns do appear in some electrodes (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4), clearly demonstrating that temporal and amplitude codes for VOT are not mutually exclusive (see also temporal encoding patterns in onset latencies of V+ electrodes; Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of local field potential data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The amplitude of the peak high-gamma (and, in many cases, of the LFP) response emerged as a robust representation of voicing category and of VOT.
source: However, as with spectrally-defined phonetic contrasts (e.g., plosive vs. fricative; Mesgarani et al., 2014), it clear that the amplitude of the peak high-gamma (and, in many cases, of the LFP) response emerged as a robust representation of voicing category and of VOT.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the neural data analysis and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The fact that we found cortical sites in every participant that exhibited robust category-dependent differences in their peak response amplitude rules out the possibility that at least these neural populations are merely responding to spectral cues in the burst or voicing alone.
source: However, the fact that we found cortical sites in every participant that exhibited robust category-dependent differences in their peak response amplitude rules out the possibility that at least these neural populations are merely responding to spectral cues in the burst or voicing alone.
evidence: The claim is a logical inference drawn from the pattern of neural responses.

claim: Corrupting peak amplitude information had a devastating effect on the decoding of voicing category, while corrupting the fine temporal patterns had no measurable impact on classifier performance.
source: Notably, if either (or both) of these models – a local or ensemble temporal code – was primarily responsible for the neural representation of VOT in the high-gamma range, then the selective corruption of temporal information in a classifier (Figure 1F) should have reduced neural decoding of voicing category to chance levels, while corrupting peak amplitude information should have had little or no effect. We found the opposite pattern of results: corrupting peak amplitude information had a devastating effect on the decoding of voicing category, while corrupting the fine temporal patterns that could have discriminated between voicing categories had no measurable impact on classifier performance.
evidence: The claim summarizes the classifier results and their implications.

claim: Our work does not rule out the possibility that local or ensemble temporal codes may also play a role in the cortical representation of VOT.
source: To be clear, our work does not rule out the possibility that local or ensemble temporal codes may also play a role in the cortical representation of VOT.
evidence: The claim acknowledges limitations of the study's conclusions.

claim: Spatially-localized peak neural response amplitude is a robust code for VOT.
source: However, it does highlight spatially-localized peak neural response amplitude as a robust code for VOT.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the classifier results.

claim: There is evidence for a shared representation of both spectrally- and temporally-cued phonetic features by high-gamma responses in the human superior temporal lobe.
source: Thus, in contrast to prior work theorizing parallel, but fundamentally different, coding schemes for spectrally- and temporally-cued phonetic features (Steinschneider et al., 1999; Steinschneider et al., 2013), we demonstrate evidence for a shared representation of both by high-gamma responses in the human superior temporal lobe.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the results and contrasts with prior theories, supported by citations.

claim: The model highlights one parsimonious approach by which selectivity for either temporal gaps or coincidences could be implemented by biologically-inspired neurophysiological microcircuits.
source: Our model highlights one parsimonious approach by which selectivity for either temporal gaps or coincidences could be implemented by biologically-inspired neurophysiological microcircuits (Buonomano and Merzenich, 1995; Gao and Wehr, 2015; Eggermont, 2000; Carr, 1993; Konishi, 2003; Rauschecker, 2014; Rauschecker, 1998).
evidence: The claim describes the contribution of the computational model and is supported by citations.

claim: Gap and coincidence detector units responded to simulated voiced (/b/) and voiceless (/p/) stimuli with different response amplitudes.
source: We found that, just like in the neural data, gap and coincidence detector units responded to simulated voiced (/b/) and voiceless (/p/) stimuli with different response amplitudes.
evidence: The claim describes the model's behavior in simulations.

claim: We need not invoke any specialized temporal code to account for the representation of temporally cued phonetic features.
source: As such, we need not invoke any specialized temporal code to account for the representation of temporally cued phonetic features.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the model's ability to capture the neural data.

claim: Our results provide evidence implicating a common neural coding scheme in the neural representation of behaviorally relevant speech features, whether they are embedded within the instantaneous spectrum or the fine temporal structure of the speech signal.
source: Rather, our results provide evidence implicating a common neural coding scheme in the neural representation of behaviorally relevant speech features, whether they are embedded within the instantaneous spectrum or the fine temporal structure of the speech signal.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the overall results of the study.

claim: Different neural populations encode pitch and key properties of the speech envelope such as onsets and auditory edges.
source: Recent ECoG evidence suggests an even more expansive view of the fundamental role of spatial coding in cortical speech representation (Yi et al., 2019) in which different neural populations also encode pitch (Tang et al., 2017) and key properties of the speech envelope such as onsets and auditory edges (Hamilton et al., 2018; Oganian and Chang, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent ECoG studies.

claim: Although the neural network was only designed to discriminate between categories, graded amplitude differences in response to different VOTs emerged naturally from the same computational properties.
source: Crucially, although the neural network was only designed to discriminate between categories (i.e., gaps vs. coincidences), we also observed graded amplitude differences in response to different VOTs (Figure 2H), but only in an electrode's preferred category. These within-category patterns emerged naturally from the same computational properties that allowed the network to capture basic between-category encoding: (1) the relative responsiveness of each temporal integrator unit (Gap, Coinc) to its various inputs (burst, voicing, and inhibition); (2) the time-dependent properties inherent to neuronal activation dynamics (e.g., decay of postsynaptic potentials towards a unit's resting activation level); and (3) the nonlinear transformation of postsynaptic inputs into response outputs (rectified linear activation function controlled by a unit's propagation threshold).
evidence: The claim describes an emergent property of the model and the mechanisms responsible.

claim: This asymmetric within-category encoding scheme closely resembled the pattern observed in real neurophysiological data.
source: This asymmetric within-category encoding scheme closely resembled the pattern observed in real neurophysiological data, where peak response amplitude to VOTs within the same voicing category only differed within a neural population's preferred category (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of model outputs to neural data.

claim: Human nonprimary auditory cortex maintains a robust, graded representation of VOT that includes the sub-phonetic details about how a particular speech token was pronounced.
source: This result clearly demonstrates that human nonprimary auditory cortex maintains a robust, graded representation of VOT that includes the sub-phonetic details about how a particular speech token was pronounced (Blumstein et al., 2005; Toscano et al., 2010; Toscano et al., 2018; Frye et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the within-category encoding results and is supported by citations.

claim: Fine-grained acoustic detail has demonstrable effects on listeners' behavior.
source: Even though sub-phonetic information is not strictly necessary for mapping sound to meaning in stable, noise-free listening environments, this fine-grained acoustic detail has demonstrable effects on listeners' behavior (Kuhl, 1991; Carney, 1977; Pisoni and Tash, 1974; Massaro and Cohen, 1983; Andruski et al., 1994; McMurray et al., 2002; Schouten et al., 2003), and modern theories of speech perception agree that perceptual learning (e.g., adaptation to accented speakers) and robust cue integration would be impossible if the perception of speech sounds were strictly categorical (Miller and Volaitis, 1989; Clayards et al., 2008; Kleinschmidt and Jaeger, 2015; McMurray and Jongman, 2011; Toscano and McMurray, 2010; McClelland and Elman, 1986; Norris and McQueen, 2008; Norris et al., 2016; Magnuson et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to behavioral and theoretical work.

claim: Modern theories of speech perception agree that perceptual learning and robust cue integration would be impossible if the perception of speech sounds were strictly categorical.
source: Even though sub-phonetic information is not strictly necessary for mapping sound to meaning in stable, noise-free listening environments, this fine-grained acoustic detail has demonstrable effects on listeners' behavior (Kuhl, 1991; Carney, 1977; Pisoni and Tash, 1974; Massaro and Cohen, 1983; Andruski et al., 1994; McMurray et al., 2002; Schouten et al., 2003), and modern theories of speech perception agree that perceptual learning (e.g., adaptation to accented speakers) and robust cue integration would be impossible if the perception of speech sounds were strictly categorical (Miller and Volaitis, 1989; Clayards et al., 2008; Kleinschmidt and Jaeger, 2015; McMurray and Jongman, 2011; Toscano and McMurray, 2010; McClelland and Elman, 1986; Norris and McQueen, 2008; Norris et al., 2016; Magnuson et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to theoretical work on speech perception.

claim: The same spatial/amplitude code that is implicated in the representation of phonetic information can also accommodate the representation of sub-phonetic information in the speech signal.
source: Crucially, these data suggest that the same spatial/amplitude code that is implicated in the representation of phonetic information (from spectral or temporal cues) can also accommodate the representation of sub-phonetic information in the speech signal.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the within-category encoding results.

claim: Response onset latencies of V- electrodes were time-locked to the burst.
source: The onset latency results (Figure 3) established an entirely novel correspondence between the real and simulated results that extended beyond the peak response window. Response onset latencies of V- electrodes were time-locked to the burst (Figures 2B and 3), while responses of V+ electrodes were time-locked to voicing onset (Figures 2C and 3).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of onset latency data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Responses of V+ electrodes were time-locked to voicing onset.
source: The onset latency results (Figure 3) established an entirely novel correspondence between the real and simulated results that extended beyond the peak response window. Response onset latencies of V- electrodes were time-locked to the burst (Figures 2B and 3), while responses of V+ electrodes were time-locked to voicing onset (Figures 2C and 3).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of onset latency data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The fact that the model's prediction is borne out in the neural data in STG is consistent with local temporal integration in STG.
source: The model's gap and coincidence detectors (Gap, Coinc) are designed to directly simulate neural populations in the STG. Their inputs from the burst and voicing detectors are only spectrally processed, so in the model, the temporal onset latency dynamics (Figure 2F/G) first arise in Gap and Coinc. As such, the fact that the model's prediction is borne out in the neural data in STG (Figure 2B, C and 3) is consistent with local temporal integration in STG.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the correspondence between model predictions and neural data.

claim: The model provides an explicit, mathematical account of multiple seemingly disparate observations about the neurophysiological data.
source: Overall, the results of these model simulations illustrate how the same network properties that transform temporal cues into a spatial code are also able to naturally explain at least three additional patterns observed within category-selective neural populations: (1) the graded encoding of VOT within a population's preferred category; (2) the lack of graded encoding of VOT within a population's non-preferred category; and (3) the early temporal dynamics of neural responses, which depend on a population's category-selectivity. Thus, the model provides an explicit, mathematical account of multiple seemingly disparate observations about the neurophysiological data, all of which arise directly from a parsimonious implementation of gap- and coincidence-detection with well-established, theoretically-motivated neuronal circuits.
evidence: The claim summarizes the explanatory power of the computational model.

claim: The model predicted VOT-dependence in the latency of the peak response in both Gap and Coinc units, but we did not find evidence for these fine-grained patterns in the high-gamma data.
source: While the model captured several notable features of the neural data (including some for which it was not explicitly designed), we observed at least one inconsistency between the simulated and real neural responses. The model predicted VOT-dependence in the latency of the peak response in both Gap and Coinc units (Figure 2F/G), but we did not find evidence for these fine-grained patterns in the high-gamma data (Figure 2B/C; see also lack of category-dependent temporal patterns during peak window: Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim describes a discrepancy between model predictions and neural data.

claim: VOT-sensitive neural populations were scattered throughout posterior and middle superior temporal gyrus with no discernible topographical map of selectivity or evidence for lateralized asymmetries.
source: As with tuning for spectrally-cued phonetic features (Mesgarani et al., 2014; Hamilton et al., 2018) (e.g., plosives vs. fricatives), VOT-sensitive neural populations in the present study were scattered throughout posterior and middle superior temporal gyrus with no discernible topographical map of selectivity or evidence for lateralized asymmetries (Liégeois-Chauvel et al., 1999; Zatorre and Belin, 2001), although data limitations prevent us from ruling out this possibility entirely (for detailed results, see Material and methods).
evidence: The claim is based on spatial analysis of electrode locations and is supported by citations.

claim: There exist complex associations between VOT and the amplitude/temporal information carried in lower-frequency ranges.
source: Indeed, it is clear from the exploratory analyses of auditory evoked local field potentials (Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4) that there do exist complex associations between VOT and the amplitude/temporal information carried in lower-frequency ranges.
evidence: The claim is based on exploratory analyses of local field potential data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Neural responses to different VOT tokens that are members of the same voicing category can only be considered truly categorical if the responses are indiscriminable.
source: Finally, it is critical to distinguish our results from studies describing neural correlates of categorical speech perception, per se (e.g., Chang et al., 2010). Neural responses to different VOT tokens that are members of the same voicing category can only be considered truly categorical if the responses are indiscriminable (e.g., Liberman et al., 1957; Macmillan et al., 1977).
evidence: The claim defines what would constitute truly categorical neural responses and is supported by citations.

claim: Acoustically distinct members of the same phonetic category are distinguishable in neural populations that are selective for that voicing category.
source: In our results, acoustically distinct members of the same phonetic category are distinguishable in neural populations that are selective for that voicing category (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on the within-category encoding results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The present results are best interpreted as elucidating neural mechanisms of category perception, but not necessarily categorical perception, of voiced vs. voiceless stop consonants.
source: In light of this graded VOT representation, the present results are best interpreted as elucidating neural mechanisms of category perception, but not necessarily categorical perception, of voiced vs. voiceless stop consonants.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the results in the context of categorical perception theory.

claim: The model suggests that top-down effects may not be a necessary condition for explaining the observed non-linear encoding patterns.
source: While limited coverage beyond the superior temporal lobe precludes us from ruling out the influence of top-down categorical perception (Lee et al., 2012; Myers et al., 2009; Evans and Davis, 2015) (possibly originating in frontal cortex; Sohoglu et al., 2012; Leonard et al., 2016; Cope et al., 2017; Park et al., 2015) on our results, it is notable that the model we present (which does not posit top-down effects) suggests that top-down effects may not be a necessary condition for explaining the observed non-linear encoding patterns (see also McClelland et al., 2006; McQueen et al., 2006; Norris et al., 2000; McClelland and Elman, 1986; Norris and McQueen, 2008).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the model's ability to capture the data without top-down mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Spatially-discrete neural populations in human auditory cortex are tuned to detect either gaps or coincidences between spectral cues.
source: In conclusion, the present results show that spatially-discrete neural populations in human auditory cortex are tuned to detect either gaps or coincidences between spectral cues, and these sites simultaneously represent both phonetic and sub-phonetic information carried by VOT, a temporal speech cue found in almost all languages (Lisker and Abramson, 1964; Cho and Ladefoged, 1999).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings and is supported by citations.

claim: These sites simultaneously represent both phonetic and sub-phonetic information carried by VOT.
source: In conclusion, the present results show that spatially-discrete neural populations in human auditory cortex are tuned to detect either gaps or coincidences between spectral cues, and these sites simultaneously represent both phonetic and sub-phonetic information carried by VOT, a temporal speech cue found in almost all languages (Lisker and Abramson, 1964; Cho and Ladefoged, 1999).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings.

claim: This demonstrates a common (spatial) neural code in STG that accounts for the representation of behaviorally relevant phonetic features embedded within the spectral and temporal structure of speech.
source: This demonstrates a common (spatial) neural code in STG that accounts for the representation of behaviorally relevant phonetic features embedded within the spectral and temporal structure of speech.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the overall results of the study.

claim: Our findings add to a growing body of work highlighting the critical role of human STG as a sensory-perceptual computational hub in the human speech perception system.
source: In this way, our findings also add to a growing body of work highlighting the critical role of human STG as a sensory-perceptual computational hub in the human speech perception system (Yi et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2010; Leonard et al., 2016; DeWitt and Rauschecker, 2012; Obleser and Eisner, 2009; Leonard and Chang, 2014; Sjerps et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion about the broader significance of the findings and is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Seven human participants with self-reported normal hearing were implanted with high-density multi-electrode cortical ECoG surface arrays as part of their clinical treatment for epilepsy.
source: A total of seven human participants with self-reported normal hearing were implanted with high-density (128 or 256 electrodes; 4 mm pitch) multi-electrode cortical ECoG surface arrays as part of their clinical treatment for epilepsy.
evidence: The claim describes the participant population and recording method.

claim: For all patients who participated in this study, coverage included peri-Sylvian regions of the lateral left (n = 3) or right (n = 4) hemisphere, including the superior temporal gyrus (STG).
source: For all patients who participated in this study, coverage included peri-Sylvian regions of the lateral left (n = 3) or right (n = 4) hemisphere, including the superior temporal gyrus (STG).
evidence: The claim describes the electrode coverage in the participants.

claim: All participants gave their written informed consent before the surgery and affirmed it at the start of each recording session.
source: All participants gave their written informed consent before the surgery and affirmed it at the start of each recording session.
evidence: The claim describes the ethical procedures followed in the study.

claim: The study protocol was approved by the University of California San Francisco Committee on Human Research.
source: The study protocol was approved by the University of California San Francisco Committee on Human Research.
evidence: The claim describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Data from two additional participants were excluded from analyses because of excessive epileptiform activity (artifacts) during recording sessions.
source: Data from two additional participants were excluded from analyses because of excessive epileptiform activity (artifacts) during recording sessions.
evidence: The claim describes the exclusion criteria applied to the data.

claim: Stimuli were generated with a parallel/cascade Klatt-synthesizer KLSYN88a using a 20 kHz sampling frequency.
source: Stimuli (Figure 1B) were generated with a parallel/cascade Klatt-synthesizer KLSYN88a using a 20 kHz sampling frequency (5 ms frame width in parameter tracks).
evidence: The claim describes the stimulus generation method.

claim: All stimulus parameters were identical across stimuli, with the exception of the time at which the amplitude of voicing began to increase.
source: All stimulus parameters were identical across stimuli, with the exception of the time at which the amplitude of voicing began to increase (in 10 ms steps from 0 ms to 50 ms after burst onset; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim describes the stimulus control used in the study.

claim: The total duration of each stimulus was 300 ms regardless of VOT.
source: The total duration of each stimulus was 300 ms regardless of VOT.
evidence: The claim describes a property of the stimuli.

claim: The onset noise-burst was 2 ms in duration and had constant spectral properties across all stimuli.
source: The onset noise-burst was 2 ms in duration and had constant spectral properties across all stimuli.
evidence: The claim describes a property of the stimuli.

claim: Four of seven participants simultaneously performed a behavioral task wherein they indicated on each trial whether they heard 'ba' or 'pa' using a touchscreen tablet.
source: Four of seven participants simultaneously performed a behavioral task wherein they indicated on each trial whether they heard 'ba' or 'pa' using a touchscreen tablet (programmed using a custom MATLAB GUI).
evidence: The claim describes the behavioral task performed by some participants.

claim: Individual trials were excluded from behavioral analysis if a participant did not make a response or if the participant's reaction time was more than three standard deviations from the participant's mean reaction time.
source: For the four participants who participated in the behavioral identification task, individual trials were excluded from behavioral analysis if a participant did not make a response or if the participant's reaction time was more than three standard deviations from the participant's mean reaction time.
evidence: The claim describes the trial exclusion criteria for behavioral analysis.

claim: Behavioral response data were submitted to mixed effects logistic regression with a fixed effect of VOT and random intercepts for participants.
source: Behavioral response data were submitted to mixed effects logistic regression with a fixed effect of VOT (coded as a continuous variable) and random intercepts for participants, allowing individual participants to vary in their voicing category boundary.
evidence: The claim describes the statistical analysis method used for behavioral data.

claim: Voltage fluctuations were recorded and amplified with a multichannel amplifier optically connected to a digital signal acquisition system sampling at approximately 3051.78 Hz.
source: Voltage fluctuations were recorded and amplified with a multichannel amplifier optically connected to a digital signal acquisition system (Tucker-Davis Technologies) sampling at approximately 3051.78 Hz.
evidence: The claim describes the neural recording method.

claim: Line noise was removed via notch filtering (60 Hz and harmonics at 120 and 180 Hz).
source: Line noise was removed via notch filtering (60 Hz and harmonics at 120 and 180 Hz) and the resulting time series for each session was visually inspected to exclude channels with excessive noise.
evidence: The claim describes the preprocessing steps applied to the neural data.

claim: The analytic amplitude of the high-gamma (HG; 70–150 Hz) frequency band was extracted by averaging across eight logarithmically-spaced bands with the Hilbert transform.
source: The analytic amplitude of the high-gamma (HG; 70–150 Hz) frequency band was extracted by averaging across eight logarithmically-spaced bands with the Hilbert transform as described elsewhere (Mesgarani et al., 2014; Sjerps et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim describes the method for extracting high-gamma activity and is supported by citations.

claim: The HG signal was down-sampled to 400 Hz, providing temporal resolution to observe latency effects on the order of <10 ms.
source: The HG signal was down-sampled to 400 Hz, providing temporal resolution to observe latency effects on the order of <10 ms (the spacing of the VOTs of among the six experimental stimuli).
evidence: The claim describes the temporal resolution of the neural data analysis.

claim: An electrode was included in analyses if it was anatomically located on the lateral temporal lobe and the electrode's grand mean HG exceeded one standard deviation of the baseline window's HG activity.
source: An electrode was included in our analyses if (1) it was anatomically located on the lateral temporal lobe (either superior or middle temporal gyrus), and (2) the electrode's grand mean HG (across all trials and timepoints during a window 100–300 ms after stimulus onset) exceeded one standard deviation of the baseline window's HG activity.
evidence: The claim describes the electrode selection criteria.

claim: Across all seven participants, 346 electrodes met the criteria for speech-responsive electrodes.
source: Across all seven participants, 346 electrodes met these criteria (speech-responsive electrodes; Supplementary file 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim reports the number of electrodes meeting the selection criteria.

claim: To identify VOT-sensitive electrodes, we computed the nonparametric correlation coefficient (Spearman's ρ) across trials between VOT and peak HG amplitude.
source: To identify electrodes where the peak response depended on stimulus VOT (VOT-sensitive electrodes), we computed the nonparametric correlation coefficient (Spearman's ρ) across trials between VOT and peak HG amplitude.
evidence: The claim describes the method for identifying VOT-sensitive electrodes.

claim: This procedure identified 49 VOT-sensitive electrodes across all seven participants.
source: This procedure identified 49 VOT-sensitive electrodes across all seven participants (p<0.05; Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim reports the number of VOT-sensitive electrodes identified.

claim: Across VOT-sensitive electrodes, the mean peak occurred 198.8 ms after stimulus onset (SD = 42.3 ms).
source: Across VOT-sensitive electrodes, the mean peak occurred 198.8 ms after stimulus onset (SD = 42.3 ms).
evidence: The claim reports the timing of the peak neural response.

claim: 76% of the VOT-sensitive electrodes were located posterior to the lateral extent of the transverse temporal sulcus.
source: Of the 49 VOT-sensitive electrodes, 76% were located posterior to the lateral extent of the transverse temporal sulcus (defined as y ≥ 6 in MNI coordinate space based on projection of the sulcus onto the lateral STG in the left hemisphere).
evidence: The claim reports the spatial distribution of VOT-sensitive electrodes.

claim: There was no significant difference in the localization of voiceless-selective versus voiced-selective electrodes along either the anterior-posterior axis or the dorsal-ventral axis.
source: Mann-Whitney rank-sum tests showed that there was no significant difference in the localization of voiceless-selective (V-) versus voiced-selective (V+) electrodes along either the anterior-posterior axis (y-dimension in MNI coordinate space; U = 342, z = −1.23, p=0.22) or the dorsal-ventral axis (z-dimension in MNI coordinate space; U = 414, z = 0.29, p=0.77).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical tests on electrode locations.

claim: There was no difference in the rate of VOT-sensitive sites or in the proportion of VOT-sensitive sites that were selective for each category as a function of hemisphere.
source: Pearson's χ2 tests confirmed there was no difference in the rate of VOT-sensitive sites (χ2(1)=0.15, p=0.70) or in the proportion of VOT-sensitive sites that were selective for each category (χ2(1)=1.74, p=0.19) as a function of hemisphere.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical tests on hemispheric differences.

claim: We found no evidence that the observed spatial/amplitude code reflected any topographical organization nor any lateralized asymmetries in the encoding of VOT.
source: Thus, consistent with past ECoG work examining spatial patterns of STG encoding for other phonetic features (e.g., Hamilton et al., 2018) we found no evidence that the observed spatial/amplitude code reflected any topographical organization nor any lateralized asymmetries in the encoding of VOT, although data limitations prevent us from ruling out this possibility entirely.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from spatial analyses and is supported by citation to prior work.
